name: Emeka Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I milk a hundred and forty cows twice a day, at five in the morning and four in the afternoon, in a herringbone parlour my father-in-law built in 1987. Between milkings it's scraping the yards, feeding silage, seeing to any lame cows and dealing with whatever's broken. The milk tanker comes every other day, and the milk goes to a big dairy company that pays us by the litre.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet of the morning milking, the cows coming in in the same order every day, the same old girl always first through the gate. What wears me out is the milk price and the paperwork. The government sends forms about slurry, forms about medicines, forms about forms, and my wife Grace does most of them at night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who else is on the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My son Tobi works with me, he's twenty-nine, and he'll take it on when I stop. We go to chapel on Sunday, then it's milking again, because cows don't know what day it is. My daughter's a primary teacher, married, with two little ones I see too little of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the next five years, one at a time. Here's the first. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let it stay a tool, and let people get on with honest work. I'd say it after chapel, if anyone asked, but most of the men there don't care about computers. I don't go online, so that's where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes nothing for me. The cows still need milking at five, and the milk price is set by the dairy company and the market, not by any search engine. If anything matters, it's the government's rules, and those keep coming whatever happens with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep the parlour going, fix it myself when it breaks, and keep the bank happy. We've got maybe two or three weeks of money if the milk cheque is late, so I'd not spend anything I didn't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. This is the world I know, and I'm content in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government's rules keep coming. Which ones bother you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The slurry rules. They tell us when we can spread and how much, and then they change it, and we have to build a bigger store we can't afford. I'm not against looking after the river, I fish in it, but a man in an office who's never seen a slurry pit shouldn't be deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the milk cheque is late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It happened once, when the dairy changed its computer system and everyone got paid a fortnight late. I had to ring the feed man and ask him to wait, which I'd never done before. He said he'd had six calls that morning already.

S0.say: I'd say let it stay a tool and let people get on with honest work. I'd say it after chapel if asked, but I don't go online.
S0.think: I really think it changes nothing, because the cows still need milking at five and the dairy sets the price. What matters is government rules, which keep coming regardless.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as before, keeping the old parlour running and fixing it himself. Spends nothing he doesn't have to, with only two or three weeks of money if the milk cheque is late.
S0.feel: Steady and content in the world he knows.
S0.quote: I'm not against looking after the river, I fish in it, but a man in an office who's never seen a slurry pit shouldn't be deciding.
S0.fieldNote: His grievance is with government rules, not technology or the market. A late milk cheque caused by the dairy's new computer system left a lasting impression. Faith and routine run through everything he says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, slow is the right speed for anything. I'd say farming has always changed slowly and that's why it lasts. And I'd say the young ones should learn the trade properly, with their hands, before they learn computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'll be retired before it touches the parlour, and Tobi can decide what to do with it. The part about fewer beginners bothers me, though. I learned from my father-in-law, standing next to him in the pit for years, and that's how it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd make sure Tobi learns everything I know, the cows' names, which ones kick, how to tell a cow is about to calve from the way she stands. I'd push for the young farmers' club to bring back apprenticeships, maybe write to the agricultural college. I wouldn't buy anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content for myself, and a bit worried for the next lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said learn with their hands first. Does Tobi use any of the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's got an app on his phone that tells him when the cows are on heat, from collars on their necks. I'll admit it's useful, he caught three I'd have missed last spring. But he still walks the cows every morning, because I told him the app doesn't know the cow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an apprenticeship look like, to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A young person living near the farm, working alongside an older farmer for three or four years, paid a fair wage and learning everything. Not a classroom, a cowshed. My father-in-law didn't have a certificate in teaching, but he taught me better than any college.

S1.say: I'd say slow is the right speed, because farming changes slowly and that's why it lasts. Young people should learn the trade with their hands before computers.
S1.think: I really think I'll retire before it touches the parlour, and Tobi can decide. Fewer beginners bothers me, because I learned standing beside my father-in-law for years.
S1.do: Makes sure Tobi learns everything, from the cows' names to the signs of calving. Pushes the young farmers' club to bring back apprenticeships and writes to the agricultural college, while buying nothing new.
S1.feel: Content for himself and a bit worried for the next generation.
S1.quote: He still walks the cows every morning, because I told him the app doesn't know the cow.
S1.fieldNote: He grudgingly credits Tobi's heat-detection collars, but insists on the morning walk. His traditional values show in his push for real apprenticeships over classrooms. He sees learning the trade by hand as how farming lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a hard lesson for people in offices, and they'll have to find honest work like the rest of us. I'd say the politicians arguing won't fix anything, they never do. People should look after their own and their neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's not my problem directly, but it's my daughter's husband's problem, he works in insurance. And the dairy company's office, where the cheques come from, might be all machines by then. I don't trust that after the late cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son-in-law to look at a trade, plumbing or electrics, something with his hands. I'd keep milking as normal. And I'd ask Grace to keep a paper record of every milk delivery, so if the dairy's machine got it wrong, we'd have proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, for the family. Not for the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell your son-in-law to learn a trade. How would that go down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd probably say he's too old to start again at thirty-four. But my own father started a new trade at forty when the mill closed. Nobody gave him money for it, he just got up and did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should look after their own. What if their own can't help them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the church and the village should. That's what they're for. The government is the last resort, not the first.

S2.say: I'd say it's a hard lesson for office people and they'll need to find honest work like the rest of us. Politicians arguing won't fix it; people should look after their own and their neighbours.
S2.think: I really think it's not directly my problem, but my son-in-law in insurance could be hit. I don't trust a dairy office run by machines after the late cheque.
S2.do: Urges his son-in-law to learn a hands-on trade like plumbing or electrics. Keeps milking as normal and asks Grace to keep a paper record of every milk delivery as proof against the dairy's systems.
S2.feel: A bit uneasy for the family, not for the cows.
S2.quote: The government is the last resort, not the first.
S2.fieldNote: His traditional view puts family, church and village before the state. He'd answer job loss with self-help, citing his father's new trade at forty. The paper record shows his deep distrust of systems he can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people making all this money should stop arguing and remember there's more to life than shares. I'd say the gains should go to people who work, through jobs and training, not handouts. And I'd say a country that can still milk its own cows will be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried about the house prices, because Tobi will never be able to buy the farm off us at that price. We'd have to leave it to him, and that's complicated with my daughter's share. And my son-in-law would be out of work, which hurts my daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Grace and a solicitor in the first six months and sort out how Tobi gets the farm, fairly to my daughter too. I'd keep milking. I'd offer my son-in-law work on the farm if he needed it, even just a few days a week, so he's doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for the family. The farm itself would be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you be fair to your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up. If Tobi gets the farm and the farm's worth a fortune on paper, my daughter gets very little by comparison. We'd probably have to give her part of the land or a share in it, and hope they never fall out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your son-in-law working on the farm. Would he want that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not at first. He's an office man, he's never milked a cow. But a man with nothing to do loses himself, and I'd rather he was scraping yards than sitting at home.

S3.say: I'd say the people making money should remember there's more to life than shares. Gains should go to working people through jobs and training, not handouts.
S3.think: I'm privately worried that booming prices mean Tobi can never buy the farm. Leaving it to him gets complicated with my daughter's share, and my son-in-law would be out of work.
S3.do: Sits down with Grace and a solicitor within six months to plan how Tobi inherits the farm fairly to his daughter too. Keeps milking and offers his son-in-law a few days a week on the farm.
S3.feel: Anxious for the family, though the farm itself would be fine.
S3.quote: But a man with nothing to do loses himself, and I'd rather he was scraping yards than sitting at home.
S3.fieldNote: The threat here is to fairness within the family, not to the farm. He'd offer work rather than money, true to his views. Rising land value turns into an inheritance problem, which keeps him up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too far, and a farm isn't a factory. I'd say a man should be allowed to milk his own cows without being forced into debt for a robot. I'd say it at chapel and to the dairy, if they tried to make us change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, milking robots already exist, and the neighbour's gone into debt for two of them. If the big farms all had robots for everything, the milk price would fall and the dairy would only want the big farms. We'd be squeezed out, unless Tobi takes on a loan I'd never want him to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tobi not to borrow for robots, not while I'm alive. I'd keep milking in the parlour and look for a smaller dairy that wants traditional milk, maybe for cheese, in the first year. And I'd pray about it, honestly, because some things you can't fix with a spanner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. This is the one that could end what three generations built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your neighbour.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My neighbour bought two milking robots and now the bank milks him. He works longer than I do, fixing them in the middle of the night when they break, and the cows don't go out on the grass anymore. He's a good man and he's tired all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Tobi disagreed with you about the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd argue, and in the end it'd be his choice, because it'll be his farm. I'd tell him what I think, and then I'd pray he's right. A father can't hold on forever.

S4.say: I'd say this goes too far, because a farm isn't a factory. A man should be able to milk his own cows without being forced into debt for a robot.
S4.think: I really think robots everywhere would drop the milk price, and the dairy would only want big farms. We'd be squeezed out unless Tobi took on a loan I'd never want.
S4.do: Tells Tobi not to borrow for robots and keeps milking in the parlour. Looks in the first year for a smaller dairy, perhaps a cheesemaker, that wants traditional milk, and prays about it.
S4.feel: Alarmed, because this could end what three generations built.
S4.quote: My neighbour bought two milking robots and now the bank milks him.
S4.fieldNote: His neighbour's tiring life with robots is his warning. He'd resist, but he admits the farm will be Tobi's to decide. Faith is part of his plan, alongside a practical search for a cheese dairy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, the last one. What would help is a fair milk price and an apprenticeship scheme, so young people can learn the trade properly and stay on the land. Not handouts. Just a fair chance to keep doing honest work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. They know me. If a robot milks them, they'll get used to it, I suppose, but something goes out of the place when nobody stands in the pit with them at five in the morning.

headlineQuote: My neighbour bought two milking robots and now the bank milks him.
portrait: Emeka is 58 and milks a hundred and forty cows twice a day in a parlour his father-in-law built, with his son Tobi set to take over. He never uses AI, distrusts systems after a late milk cheque, and blames government paperwork more than technology or markets. Through the office pictures his worries are family ones: his son-in-law's insurance job and how to pass the farm on fairly. The robot picture alarms him, because his neighbour is deep in debt for milking robots, and he'd rather pray and find a cheese dairy than borrow.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because falling milk prices and debt for robots could end what three generations built.
whatWouldHelp: A fair milk price and an apprenticeship scheme so young people can learn the trade properly and stay on the land, not handouts.
